steps.t: Count to 10 Press + to put a counter in the frame. Count out loud with me. Then press Mix them up . Is it still the same number? 0 zero − + Mix them up Press the plus to put a counter in the frame. Count out loud with me. Then press Mix them up. Is it still the same number? Counting is saying one number for each thing, and never saying two numbers for the same thing. Press the plus. One counter appears, and we say one. Press again. Two. Each press puts exactly one counter in a hole and we say exactly one number. When the frame is full we have said ten. Children rush and say numbers faster than the counters appear, so the last number they say is not how many there are. So press once, say one number, then wait. Let your voice keep up with your finger. Then press Mix them up. The counters move to new holes, but no counter comes or goes, so the number stays the same.

See how many Press Look! The pattern shows for a moment. Tap how many you saw, without counting. Look! Do not count! Press look, see the pattern, then tap how many you saw. You do not always have to count. Some patterns you can just see. Press look. The counters flash up in a pattern, like the dots on a dice, and then they are gone. Five in a dice pattern looks like five. You did not count it. You recognised it. Children panic when the pattern disappears and guess wildly. You saw it. Trust the picture in your head. So press look, hold the picture, then tap what you saw.

Then to 20 Fill the first frame. That is 10 . Then keep going: 10 and 1 more is 11. 0 zero − + Fill the first frame. That is ten. Then keep going. Ten and one more is eleven. After ten we do not start again. We keep the ten and add the rest on. Fill the first frame right up. That is ten. Now put one counter in the second frame. Ten and one more is eleven. Another. Ten and two is twelve. All the way to twenty, which is two full frames. Children think the second frame starts a new count and say one again. It does not. The ten is still there, sitting in the first frame. So say ten and, then count the loose ones on top.

Read the number Look at the counters. Which number is it? Tap it. Look at the counters. Which number is it? Tap the number. Every amount of counters has one number that names it. Look at the frame. One full row and three more. That is thirteen. Now find thirteen among the numbers and tap it. The counters and the number are two ways of saying exactly the same thing. Children tap a number that looks like the one they want. Thirteen and thirty sound alike and look alike at a glance. So count the counters first, say the number out loud, then look for that number.

Write the number Press the keys to write the number. Clear Now write the number. Press the digit keys to build it. Writing a number means choosing its digits and putting them in the right order. For fourteen you press one, then four. The one is not saying one. It is saying one whole ten. The four beside it is the four loose ones. Children press the digits in the order they hear them, and forty one comes out instead of fourteen. The tens digit goes first, on the left. So count the full frames first and press that digit. Then count the loose ones and press that.

Zero means none Press Take one away until the plate is empty. 5 Take one away Take the counters away one at a time. When there are none left, that is zero. Zero is a number, and it means there are none at all. Take the counters away one at a time. Three. Two. One. Now take the last one. The frame is empty, and the number for an empty frame is zero. Not nothing, not blank. Zero. Children think zero means the counting stopped, or that it is not really a number. It is a number, and it has its own place at the very start of the number line. So take them away one by one and say the number each time, right down to zero.

Counting in tens A full frame is one ten . Press Next ten and count in tens: 10, 20. 0 Next ten A full frame is one ten. Press next ten and count in tens: ten, twenty. Counting in tens works the same way, in bigger steps. One full frame is one ten. Press next ten and another full frame appears. Ten. Twenty. Thirty. Each press is a whole frame of ten, not one counter. Children count the frames as ones, and say one, two, three instead of ten, twenty, thirty. Each frame is worth ten all by itself. So say ten every time a new frame appears, and count them in tens.

Counting in twos Socks come in pairs . Press Next pair and count in twos with me: 2, 4, 6… 0 Next pair Socks come in pairs. Press next pair and count in twos with me: two, four, six. Counting in twos means saying every second number and skipping the ones between. Socks come in pairs, and a pair is two. Press next pair. Two. Again. Four. Again. Six. You are counting the socks, but two at a time, so it is much quicker than counting them one by one. Children say the numbers in between out of habit. In twos you go two, four, six. Three and five are skipped over. So say it out loud with me and let the rhythm carry you. Two, four, six, eight, ten.

steps.g: division odd and even statistics subtraction
steps.t: Odd and even Tap a number. If every counter has a partner , the number is even . If one is left alone, it is odd . Sort 8 numbers. Tap a number. If every counter has a partner, the number is even. If one is left alone, it is odd. An even number can be split into pairs with nobody left out. An odd number always has one left over. Take six. Pair them up. Two, two, two. Everybody has a partner, so six is even. Now take seven. Pair them up and one counter is standing on its own with nobody to go with. So seven is odd. Children guess by whether the number looks big or small. Size has nothing to do with it. Only the pairing does. So pair them up and look for one left over.

More or fewer? Which group has more ? Tap it. Which group has more? Tap it. More means a bigger amount. Fewer means a smaller one. Two groups on the screen. Match them up, one from this group with one from that group. When one group runs out first, the other group has more. If they run out together, they are the same. Children choose the group that takes up more room. Six big things spread out is still fewer than eight little things squeezed together. So pair them off one to one and see which group still has some left.

Put them in order Tap the cards from the smallest to the biggest . New cards Tap the cards from the smallest number to the biggest. Putting numbers in order means starting at the smallest and working up. Look at all the cards and find the smallest number of them all. Tap that first. Now look at what is left and find the smallest of those. Tap that. Keep going and the cards line up in order. Children order the cards by how they are arranged on the screen, or start from the biggest. Read the numbers, not the positions. So each time, ask which of the ones still left is smallest.

Numbers to 20 Two numbers. Which one is bigger ? Tap it. The number line will help you. Two numbers. Which one is bigger? Tap it. The number line will help you. The number line settles any argument about which number is bigger. Find both numbers on the line. The one further to the right is the bigger one, every time. Fifteen sits to the right of nine, so fifteen is bigger. Children compare the digits and pick the one that looks longer or louder. Nine has a big digit but it sits well to the left of fifteen. So find both numbers on the line, and tap the one further along.

Compare to 20 Two pictures. Does the first one have more , fewer , or the same ? Look at the tens first, then the ones. Two pictures. Does the first have more, fewer, or the same? Look at the tens first, then the ones. With bigger numbers, look at the tens before you look at the ones. Two pictures. Count the full frames in each. If one has two full frames and the other has one, the first one is bigger, and you can stop right there. Only if the tens match do you need to compare the loose ones. Children start with the loose ones because they are easier to see. Nine loose ones is still fewer than one full ten. So count the full frames first. If those are equal, then count the loose ones.

First, second, third Ten runners in a race. The one nearest the flag is first . Press Next runner and say the places with me. Next runner Ten runners in a race. The one nearest the flag is first. Press next runner: first, second, third. Ordinal numbers say what position something is in, not how many there are. Ten runners heading for the flag. The one nearest the flag is first. Behind them is second, then third. Press next runner and follow them all the way to tenth. Children mix up first and one. One tells you how many. First tells you where in the line. There is one runner in first place. So find the flag, then count back from the runner nearest to it.

Guess, then count Don't count yet! How many stars do you think there are? Tap your guess. New stars Do not count yet! How many stars do you think there are? Tap your guess. An estimate is a sensible guess made before you count. Look at the stars for a moment. Do not count. Does it look like about five, or about ten, or about twenty? Say the closest one. That is your estimate. Then count and see how near you were. Children think a guess has to be exactly right and freeze. An estimate is allowed to be a bit out. Being close is the whole job. So look, say the first sensible number that comes to mind, then count to check.

Estimate to 20 How many apples? Slide your guess on the number line and lock it. Then tap each apple to count it into the frames. My guess: 10 Lock my guess New apples How many apples? Slide your guess on the number line and lock it. Then tap each apple to count it into the frames. You can estimate on a number line by sliding to about the right place. Look at the apples. If it seems like more than ten but not as many as twenty, slide to somewhere near fifteen and lock it in. Then tap each apple one at a time and count. Compare your guess with the real count. Children slide to a number they like rather than one that fits the picture. Look at the apples first, then move the slider to match what you saw. So look, slide, lock, then count and compare.

Patterns you know Press Look! The picture shows for a moment. Say how many straight away, without counting. Next question Press look. The picture shows for a moment. Then tap how many you saw, without counting. Some patterns you see so often that you know them straight away. Five fingers on one hand. Five dots in a row, and more underneath. A domino with a four and a two. Look for the parts you know, then put them together: four and two make six, without counting one at a time. Children try to count every dot, one by one, and the picture hides before they finish. You do not need to. Find a part you already know, like five, and add on the rest. So press look, find the parts you know, and tap your answer.

Zero means empty Zero means none at all. Tap the answer. Next question Zero means none at all. Look at each picture and tap the answer. Zero is the number for none at all. An empty plate has zero mangoes. An empty ten frame has zero counters. If you have three sweets and eat all three, you have zero left. We write zero like this: 0. Children sometimes think zero is not a number, because there is nothing to count. It is a number. It is the number that says none, and it comes just before one when you count. So when you see nothing there, say zero, and tap 0.

Every other number Say every other number as you count. Tap the answer. Next question Count, and say every other number. The numbers you land on are all even, or all odd. When you count, odd and even numbers take turns. Start at zero and say every other number: zero, two, four, six, eight. Those are the even numbers. Start at one instead: one, three, five, seven, nine. Those are the odd numbers. Even, odd, even, odd, all the way to twenty. Children think a big number must be even, or that odd means strange. Neither is true. Twenty is even and nineteen is odd, because they take turns, just like the small ones. So hop along the numbers, jumping over every other one, and see where you land.

Places in a line Count from the front: 1st , 2nd , 3rd , all the way to 10th . Tap the answer. Next question Count from the front of the line: first, second, third. Tap the answer. First, second and third tell you a place in a line, not how many there are. Always start counting at the front. The one at the front is first, then second, then third, then fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth. When we write them short, first is 1st, second is 2nd and third is 3rd. Children start counting from the wrong end, or they count the flag as first. The flag is not in the line. Start with the one standing right behind it. So point at the front one and say first, then keep going until you reach the one you want.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. No new ideas here. Every question uses something you have already done in this lesson. If it shows counters, count them. If it asks which is bigger, use the number line. If it shows a clock, look at the short hand first. Take your time. Read it, look at it, then tap.

Adding Put the two groups together. How many altogether ? Tap the answer. Put the two groups together. How many altogether? Tap the answer. Adding is putting two groups together and finding how many there are altogether. Three counters here and two counters there. Push them together into one group. Now count the whole lot. One, two, three, four, five. Three and two make five. Children count one group and forget to carry on into the other, so they answer with just one part. So push the groups together first, then count every counter in the new group.

Taking away Tap the counters to cross them out. Next one Take some away. Tap the counters to cross them out. Taking away means starting with a group and removing some of it. Seven counters. Tap three of them and they are crossed out. Now count only the ones without a line through them. Four left. Seven take away three is four. There is a second way to reach that answer, and it is called counting back. Start at seven and count back three. Six. Five. Four. Taking away and counting back are two ways of doing the same subtraction. Children count the crossed ones and answer with those. The crossed ones are the ones that have gone. The answer is what is still there. So cross out, then count only the ones still standing.

steps.g: addition measurement odd and even position subtraction
steps.t: How many more? Press Match them up . The ones with no partner are the difference . Match them up Two rows. Match them up in pairs, and the ones left over tell you how many more. How many more is a question about the difference between two rows. Line the rows up so each thing in the top row has one underneath it. Some at the end of the longer row have nobody below them. Count those. That is how many more. Children add the two rows together, because the word more sounds like adding. This is not adding. It is finding the gap between them. So pair them off, then count only the ones left over.

Making 10 Ten in a row. Tap where to split them. Find 5 different ways to make 10. Ten friends in a row. Tap where to split them. Two numbers that make ten are a number bond. Two numbers that make ten together are called a number bond. Ten friends in a row. Tap between them to split them into two groups. Split after four and you have four and six. Four and six make ten. Split after seven and you get seven and three. Also ten. Children think there is only one right way to split them. There are lots, and every one of them is a real bond as long as both parts add to ten. So split them anywhere, then count each side and check they make ten together.

Through 10 Bigger sums. First tap the answer. Then we go through 10 together, one counter at a time. Move one Next one Adding and taking away with bigger numbers. First tap the answer. Then we will go through ten together. When you go past ten, it helps to stop at ten on the way. Take eight add five. Go up to ten first. Eight needs two to reach ten, and that leaves three of the five still to add. Ten and three is thirteen. You have gone through ten instead of counting on five times. Children count on in ones and lose their place somewhere in the middle, especially past ten. So ask how many to reach ten, use them up, then add what is left over.

Doubles A ladybird has the same spots on both sides. Double means the same again. − + A ladybird has the same spots on both sides. Double means the same again. Doubling means having the same amount again. A ladybird has the same number of spots on each side. Three on the left, three on the right. Count them all. Six. So double three is six. Children add one more instead of the same again. Double three is not four. It is three and another three. So count one side, then count the same number again on the other.

Doubles to 20 Tap a double to see it in the frames. Find 5 doubles, then use them to add. Tap a double to see it in the frames. Double seven is fourteen: that is ten and four. Bigger doubles are easier if you see them as a full ten and some left over. Double seven. Seven on one side, seven on the other. Watch the frames fill. The first frame fills up to ten, and four counters land in the second. So double seven is ten and four, which is fourteen. Children count all fourteen in ones and lose track halfway. Filling the ten first gives you something solid to build on. So fill to ten, then count what is left over on top.

Money to 20 Coins! Tap coins from the purse to pay the price. Watch the total. Tray 0 sh Purse Next Coins! Tap coins from the purse to pay the price. Watch the total. Coins are worth different amounts, so you count their value, not how many coins there are. Say the price is seven. Tap a five coin and the total says five. Now tap a two and the total says seven. Two coins, but seven altogether, because each coin is worth what is written on it. Children count the coins instead of adding up what they are worth. Three coins can be worth less than one bigger coin. So watch the total as it climbs, and stop when it reaches the price.

Counting on Put the first number in your head, then count on . How many altogether ? Next question Put the bigger number in your head, then count on. Tap the answer. You do not have to count everything from one. Put the first number in your head. Say it, then count on the rest, one at a time. Six in your head, then count on three: seven, eight, nine. Nine altogether. Children start again from one and count every counter, and they lose their place. Start from the number you already know, and it is much quicker. So say the bigger number first, then count on with your fingers.

Pairs that make 10 How many more make 10 ? Look at the empty spaces. Next question Ten is a full frame. How many more make ten? Look at the empty spaces. Numbers come in pairs that make ten, and it helps to know them by heart. A ten frame shows them. Seven counters leave three empty spaces, so seven and three make ten. One and nine, two and eight, three and seven, four and six, five and five. And ten and zero. Children count the counters that are there, when the question asks about the spaces. Count the empty spaces instead. They are the number you need to make ten. So look at the gaps, and say the pair out loud: seven and three make ten.

Know your coins Look at the coins. The number on a coin says how many shillings it is worth. Next question Look at the coins. The number on each coin says how many shillings it is worth. Tap the answer. Our money is counted in shillings, and we write sh for short. Each coin has a number on it. The number tells you how many shillings the coin is worth. A ten shilling coin is worth ten, even though it is only one coin. Two five shilling coins are worth the same as one ten. Children think more coins always means more money. It does not. One ten shilling coin is worth more than three two shilling coins, because ten is more than six. So read the number on each coin, and add them up before you decide.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. No new ideas here. Every question uses something you have already done in this lesson. If it shows counters, count them. If it asks which is bigger, use the number line. If it shows a clock, look at the short hand first. Take your time. Read it, look at it, then tap.

Two equal parts Are the two parts equal ? Equal means exactly the same size. A half means two parts that are exactly the same size. Look at each shape and say whether the two parts are equal. This lesson stands on one word. Equal. Equal means exactly the same size. Not nearly. Exactly. Look at the square with the line straight down the middle. The left part and the right part are the same size. Swap them over and you would not notice. That is equal. Now the long shape, cut near one end. One part is fat, one is thin. Not equal. Here is where children slip up. They see two parts and say equal, because there are two. Two parts is not enough. They have to be the same size. So cover one part with your hand. Is the part left over the same size? Now tap your answer.

Cut it in half Tap the shape that is cut into two equal parts . Only one of these cuts makes two equal parts. Tap the shape that is cut fairly. A fair cut makes two parts the same size. Only one cut on the screen is fair. Take the square. A line straight down the middle leaves two parts that match. A line near the edge leaves a thin strip and a big piece. Not fair. And watch this one. A line from corner to corner on a square is fair too. It does not have to be straight down. Children often pick the cut that looks neatest, or the one that is nearly in the middle. Nearly is not enough. The two parts have to match. So cover one part with your finger. If both parts look the same size, that is the fair cut. Tap it.

Colour one half Tap one part. One of two equal parts is one half . This shape is cut into two equal parts. Tap one part to colour it. One of two equal parts is one half. The shape is already cut into two equal parts. One half means one of those two parts. One, not both. Watch. The circle has a line across the middle. Two equal parts. I colour the top part and I stop. That coloured piece is one half. If I colour the bottom part as well, I have coloured every bit of the circle. That is not a half. That is the whole shape. This is the mistake almost everybody makes. Tapping is fun, so children tap both parts. Two parts coloured is the whole shape. One part is the half. So tap one part. Just one. Then say it out loud with me. One half.

Half of a group Tap a thing to send it to a plate. Both plates must end up with the same . Half works on a group of things too. Share them onto the two plates so both plates have the same. Half is not only for shapes. You can take half of a pile of things. Two fair shares. Say there are six apples and two plates. Do not guess. Deal them out one at a time, like cards. One for this plate, one for that plate. Keep going until the pile is empty. Three on each plate. So half of six is three. Children often stop when a plate looks full, and one plate ends up with more. Half only works if both plates finish with exactly the same number. So tap one thing at a time and let the plates take turns. Empty the pile, then check they match.

Half of a number Press Share to put them in two equal rows, then count one row. Share Half of a number means sharing it into two equal rows. Press share, then read how many are in one row. Halving a number is the same job as sharing. You put the counters into two equal rows, then you read one row. Watch with eight. Press share, and the eight counters line up in two rows. Count the top row. One, two, three, four. Four in the top row. And the bottom row has four as well. Four and four make eight. So half of eight is four. Here is the trap. It is easy to count every counter and answer eight. Eight is what you started with. The answer is one row. So press share. Then put your finger on one row only and count it. That is your answer.

Halve it in your head What is half of this number? Now try without the counters. Halving is sharing into two equal parts. Same job, no counters this time. You are looking for the number that goes twice. Two of them, and they make your number. Try fourteen. Ask yourself, what number and the same number make fourteen? Try six. Six and six make twelve. Too small. Try seven. Seven and seven make fourteen. That fits. So half of fourteen is seven. Watch out for one wrong answer that looks very tempting. Taking one away is not halving. Half of fourteen is not thirteen. Thirteen is just fourteen with one gone. So say your number, then hunt for the two that match. Tap that number.

Two halves make a whole Tap the half that finishes the shape. Two halves fit back together to make one whole. Tap the half that finishes the shape. A whole shape was cut into two halves. Push those two halves back together and you get the whole shape again. Look at the piece already there. Half a circle, with a straight edge down the side. Now find the piece that fills the empty space exactly. It has to be the same size as the piece there, and the same shape. A piece of a square will never fit a circle. Children often grab a piece that is nearly right, or one that is too small. A big piece and a little piece do not make two halves. So look at the gap first. Hold that shape in your head. Then tap the piece that fits.

How many halves? Two halves make one whole . How many halves do you need? If two halves make one whole, how many halves make more wholes? Count them. Every whole takes two halves. So counting halves is really counting in twos. One two for every whole. Look at one whole circle with a line down the middle. Count the pieces. Two. So one whole needs two halves. Now three whole circles. Two, and two, and two. Point and count on. Two, four, six. Three wholes need six halves. Here is the catch. Children say three, because they can see three circles. Three is how many wholes. Halves are smaller pieces, so there are always more of them than there are wholes. So point at each whole and say two. Count on as you go. The number you land on is your answer.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. No new ideas here. Every question is something you have already done in this lesson. If the question shows you a shape, ask whether the two parts are the same size. If the question gives you a number, ask what number and the same number make it. Take your time. Read it, look at it, then tap.

What comes next? A pattern repeats . Say it out loud, then tap the bead that comes next . A pattern repeats. Say the pattern out loud, then tap the bead that comes next. A pattern is something that happens again and again in the same order. Look at the beads. Red, blue, red, blue, red. Say it out loud with me and listen to your own voice. Red, blue, red, blue, red. Your voice wants to say blue next, and it is right. The next bead is blue. Children look at the very last bead and pick a different colour, as if the pattern were taking turns. It is not taking turns. It is repeating. So say the beads out loud from the start. Let your voice run on past the end. Whatever it wants to say next, tap that.

The part that repeats Every pattern has a part that repeats . How many beads are in that part? Tap the number. Every pattern has a part that repeats. How many beads are in that part? Tap the number. Every repeating pattern is built from one small part, said over and over. Take red, blue, red, blue, red, blue. The part that repeats is red, blue. Two beads. Now take red, red, blue, red, red, blue. That part is red, red, blue. Three beads. Find where the pattern starts saying the same thing again, and stop just before it. Children count all the beads on the screen instead of the part that repeats. Six beads on the line can still be a part of two. So point at the first bead and say the colours until you hear yourself start again. Count only the beads before that.

Missing shapes A shape has fallen out of the middle . Look at the bead before the hole and the bead after it. Which one belongs? A shape has fallen out of the middle of the pattern. Look at the bead before it and the bead after it. Which one belongs in the hole? When a shape falls out of the middle, the beads on either side tell you what it was. Look at the bead just before the gap and the bead just after it. If the pattern is circle, square, circle, square, and the gap has a circle before it and a circle after it, then a square belongs in the hole. Children guess from the whole line and forget to look right next to the gap. The two closest beads are the ones with the answer in them. So put one finger on the bead before the gap and one on the bead after it. Say those two out loud, then choose what goes between.

Numbers that repeat Numbers can repeat too, just like the beads. Say the pattern out loud, then tap the number that belongs. Numbers can repeat too, just like the beads. Say the pattern out loud, then tap the number that belongs. Numbers repeat in exactly the same way beads do. Look at one, two, one, two, one. Say it out loud. Your voice wants to say two, and it is right. It works with three numbers too. Five, six, seven, five, six, seven, five. Children try to add or take away, because they see numbers and think it must be a sum. This one is not a sum. It is a pattern, the same as the beads. So say the numbers out loud from the start and let your voice run on past the end.

Missing numbers Some numbers have fallen off the track. Tap a gap , then tap the number that belongs there. Some numbers have fallen off the track. Tap a gap, then tap the number that belongs there. When numbers fall off the track, the numbers still on it show you where they go. Look at the track. One, two, gap, four, five. The numbers are going up by one each time, so the gap has three in it. Tap the gap first, then tap the number that belongs there. Children fill a gap with any number that has not been used yet. The gap does not want a spare number. It wants the number that fits between its neighbours. So look at the number just before the gap and count on from it.

Make your own Make your own. Tap 2 or 3 beads for the part that repeats, then press Repeat it . My part Clear Repeat it Make your own pattern. Tap two or three beads for the part that repeats, then press repeat it. Now you are the one making the pattern. You choose the part that repeats. Tap two or three beads. Red, blue. That is your part. Press repeat it, and the machine says your part over and over, exactly as you built it. Red, blue, red, blue, red, blue. Children tap a long line of beads with no part that repeats, then wonder why it does not look like a pattern. A pattern needs a small part that comes back. So keep it short. Two beads or three. Then press repeat it and listen to whether it sounds like a pattern.

Growing shapes These patterns grow . Each one adds another row . Count the shapes, then work out how many are in the next one. These patterns grow. Each one adds another row of shapes. Count them, then work out how many are in the next one. Some patterns do not repeat. They grow. Each one is bigger than the one before, by the same amount every time. Look along the row. The first has one square, the next has three, the next has five. Each one adds two more. So the one after five squares must have seven, because it adds two as well. Children see the shapes getting bigger and guess a much bigger number. Growing does not mean growing by any amount. It grows by the same amount every single time. So work out how many are added from the first to the second. Check it is the same from the second to the third. Then add that to the last one.

Jump patterns These patterns jump . Find the jump, then fill the gaps in order. These patterns jump. Find the jump, then fill the gaps in order. A jump pattern does not go up by one. It jumps by the same amount every time. Look at two, four, six, eight. From two to four is a jump of two. From four to six is a jump of two as well. So the jumps are twos, and the next number after eight is ten. Jumps of ten work the same way. Ten, twenty, thirty. Children fill the gaps out of order, or use a different jump halfway along. Every jump in one pattern is the same size, all the way to the end. So find the jump first, then fill the gaps from left to right, adding that jump each time.

Find the missing numbers This time nobody tells you the jump . Find two numbers next to each other to work it out, then fill the holes. This time nobody tells you the jump. Look at two numbers that are next to each other to work it out, then fill the holes. This time nobody tells you the jump. You have to find it yourself. Find two numbers sitting next to each other with no gap between them. Say five and ten. From five to ten is five, so the jump is five. Now you can fill every hole, counting on in fives. Children look at the first number and the last number and work out the difference between those. That is all the jumps added together, not one jump. So find two numbers that are neighbours. Work out the step from one to the other. That is your jump.

My own number pattern Now you make a number pattern. Pick which kind, then build it. a jump pattern a repeating pattern Start at Jump by Tap 2 or 3 numbers for the part that repeats My part Clear Build it Now you make a number pattern. Choose a jump pattern or a repeating one, then build it. Now you build a number pattern of your own, and you choose what kind. A repeating one says the same numbers over and over. One, two, three, one, two, three. A jump pattern keeps adding the same amount. Two, four, six, eight. Pick which kind you want, then build it. Children mix the two kinds together halfway through, and the pattern stops being a pattern. Choose one kind and stay with it to the end. So decide first. Repeating, or jumping. Then build the whole thing that way.

3 + ? = 7 A number is missing . Press + to add counters until you reach the answer, and count how many you added. − + Next one Three add something makes seven. Tap the plus to add counters until you reach seven, and count how many you added. The question mark is hiding a number, and your job is to find out which one. Three add something makes seven. Start with three counters. Press the plus and count on. Four, five, six, seven. Stop at seven. Now count how many you pressed. You pressed four. So the hidden number is four. Children answer seven, because seven is the biggest number they can see. Seven is the number you finish on. The answer is how many you added to get there. So count on from three, stop at seven, then count only the ones you added.

9 − ? = 4 Cross out counters until the right number is left . The crossed-out ones are the missing number. Next one Nine take away something leaves four. Cross out counters until four are left, and count the crossed ones. Taking away works the same way, but you count what you crossed out. Nine take away something leaves four. Start with nine counters. Cross one out. Eight left. Keep crossing until only four are left. Now count the crossed ones. You crossed five. So the hidden number is five. Children answer four, because four is the number left on the screen. Four is what is left over. The answer is how many you took away. So cross out until four remain, then count only the ones with a line through them.

The same on both sides The = sign means the same on both sides . Press + to add counters to the light side until the scale is level. − + Next one The equals sign means the same on both sides. Add counters to the light side until the scale is level. The equals sign does not mean here comes the answer. It means the same on both sides. Look at the scale. Five on one side and three on the other, so it tips. Add counters to the light side and watch. Four. Still tipping. Five. Now it is level. Five equals five. The two sides are the same. Children think equals means the sum is finished. It does not. It means both sides weigh the same, whatever is written on them. So add to the light side one at a time and stop the moment the scale sits level.

The number machine A number machine does the same thing to every number. Look at what goes in and what comes out. What is it doing? A number machine does the same thing to every number. Look at what goes in and what comes out. What is the machine doing? A number machine does the same thing to every number you put in. Look at what goes in and what comes out. Two goes in, five comes out. Three goes in, six comes out. Four goes in, seven comes out. Every time, the number came out three bigger. So the machine is adding three. Children look at one pair only and guess from that. One pair can fit lots of machines. Two goes in and five comes out could be add three, and it could be lots of other things. So check at least two pairs, and make sure the same thing happened to both.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. No new ideas here. Every question uses something you have already done in this lesson. If it shows beads or shapes, say the pattern out loud. If it shows numbers with a gap, find the jump first. If it has a question mark, count on or count back. Take your time. Read it, look at it, then tap.

Flat shapes This is a flat shape. Press Count the sides , then Next shape . Count the sides Next shape Here is a flat shape. Press count the sides and I will count them with you. Then press next shape. A flat shape is one you could draw on paper. It has sides and it has corners. Take the square. Press count the sides and watch each one light up as we say it. One, two, three, four. Four sides. And look where two sides meet, at each corner. Four of those as well. A triangle lights up three sides and three corners. A circle has one edge that curves all the way round, and no corners at all. Children count a corner twice, or start counting again where they began and get one too many. It is easy to lose your place going round a shape. So start at one corner and remember it. Go round once. Stop when you are back where you started.

Sort the shapes Tap every shape that follows the rule. Read the rule, then tap every shape that follows it. Sorting means picking out only the shapes that follow one rule, and leaving the rest. If the rule is four sides, then squares and rectangles go in, because they both have four. Triangles stay out, because they have three. The colour does not matter. The size does not matter. Only the rule matters. Children pick shapes that look alike, or ones they like the look of. A big red square and a small blue square both follow four sides, even though they look different. So read the rule again. Then take each shape and ask it that one question.

Solid shapes A solid shape is not flat: you can hold it in your hand. Press Next shape . Next shape A solid shape is not flat. You can hold it. Press next shape to meet them all. A solid shape is not flat. It is a thing you could pick up and hold in your hand. Press next shape to meet them. A cube is like a dice, with flat square faces. A sphere is like a ball, and it rolls. A cylinder is like a tin, flat at each end and round in the middle. A cone has a point at the top, like a party hat. Children mix up a circle and a sphere, or a square and a cube. A circle is drawn on paper. A sphere is a ball you can hold. The flat one and the solid one are not the same shape. So ask yourself, could I pick this up, or is it drawn flat.

Flat or solid? Is this shape flat or solid ? Tap the answer. Look at the shape. Is it flat, or is it solid? Tap your answer. Every shape here is either flat or solid, and you can tell by asking one question. Could you hold it in your hand and turn it over? A ball, yes, so it is solid. A triangle drawn on the page, no, so it is flat. That one question sorts every shape on the screen. A picture of a solid shape is still a picture, and that catches children out. The drawing of a cube is flat on your screen, but the shape it shows is a solid one. Think about the real thing, not the paper. So look at the shape and ask, is this a thing I could pick up.

Turn it round Press Turn it . Does the shape look the same after the turn, or different ? Turn it Press turn it. The shape makes a quarter turn. Does it look the same as before? Turning a shape moves it round without changing it. It is the same shape, just facing a different way. Press turn it and the shape swings round, the way the hand of a clock moves from twelve round to three. That is a quarter turn. A square looks exactly the same after a quarter turn, because all its sides match. A rectangle does not. It was lying down and now it is standing up. Children think a turned shape has become a new shape. It has not. Nothing was added and nothing was taken away. It only moved. So watch one corner as it turns. Follow that corner and you will see the shape is the same one.

Long, longer, longest Tap them in order. Tap the pictures in order, from the shortest to the longest. To put things in order by length, you compare them two at a time. Look at the pencil and the ruler. Line up one end of each and see which one goes further. The one that goes further is longer. Find the shortest of all, tap that first, then the next shortest, and keep going. Children compare things that are not lined up at the same end, and pick wrong. A short pencil held high can look longer than a long one lying low. So imagine both ends starting in the same place, then see which one reaches further.

Heavy and light Which one is it? Tap the answer. Two things on a balance. The heavier one goes down. Tap the answer. A balance tells you which thing is heavier without you having to guess. Put an apple on one side and a feather on the other. The side that goes down is holding the heavier thing. The side that rises is holding the lighter one. If the balance stays level, they weigh the same. Children think the bigger thing must be heavier. Size and weight are not the same. A big empty box can be lighter than a small stone. So look only at which side of the balance has gone down.

Full and empty Tap the answer. These jugs hold water. Full, empty, more or less. Tap the answer. Capacity is how much a container holds, and you can see it by looking at the water. A full jug has water right up to the top. An empty one has none at all. Between the two, one jug holds more than another if its water comes up higher, when the jugs are the same shape and size. Children say a tall jug holds more just because it is tall. A tall thin jug can hold less than a short wide one. Look at how much water is in it, not how high the jug is. So look at the water itself, and compare how much of the jug it fills.

Which tool measures it? Which tool would you use? Tap it. Every measuring tool has numbers on it. Which one would you use for this job? Tap it. Different jobs need different tools, and each tool has numbers on it for its own kind of measuring. To find out how long something is, you use a ruler or a tape. To find out how heavy, you use scales. To find out how much a jug holds, you use a measuring jug. To find out how long something takes, you use a clock. Children pick the tool they have seen most often, rather than the one for this job. A ruler cannot tell you how heavy something is, however many numbers it has on it. So ask what the question wants to know. How long, how heavy, how much, or how much time.

Where is it? Tap the word that says where it is. Where is the ball? Look at the box, then tap the word that says where the ball is. Position words say where something is compared with something else. Look at the ball and the box. If the ball sits on top, that is above. Underneath is below. Tucked inside is in. Off to one side is beside, and hidden round the back is behind. Children say the word for where they would put it, instead of where it actually is. Look at the picture in front of you and describe what you can see. So find the ball, find the box, and say out loud where the ball is compared to the box.

Faces and edges Look at the solid shape. Think about its faces and edges , flat or curved. Tap the answer. Next question Look at each solid shape. Think about its faces and its edges, then tap the answer. A face is a side of a solid shape, and an edge is where two faces meet. A cube has six flat faces, like a dice. A sphere has one curved face and no edges at all, like a ball. A cylinder has two flat circles and one curved face, like a tin. A cone has one flat circle, one curved face, and one edge where they meet. Children only count the faces they can see in the picture. A solid shape has faces at the back and underneath too. Imagine picking it up and turning it round. So hold the shape in your mind, turn it round, and count every face.

Flat shape, solid shape A flat shape is drawn on paper. A solid shape can be picked up. Tap the answer. Next question A flat shape lies on paper. A solid shape can be picked up and held. Tap the answer. Every solid shape is made of faces, and a face is a flat shape. Draw round one face of a cube and you draw a square. The square is flat, and the cube is solid. A circle is flat, like a drawing of a ball. A sphere is solid, like the ball itself. Children call a cube a square, because its faces are squares. A square is only one face. The whole cube, which you can hold, is a solid shape. So ask yourself: could I pick it up? If you could, it is solid.

Will it look the same? Imagine each shape making a turn . Does it look the same afterwards? Next question Imagine each shape turning. Which one would look exactly the same after the turn? Some shapes look exactly the same after you turn them, and some do not. A quarter turn is like the hand of a clock moving from twelve to three. A square looks the same after a quarter turn, because all its sides are the same length. A circle looks the same however far you turn it. A rectangle stands up on its end, so it looks different, until it has turned half way round. Children think every shape changes when it turns, or that every shape stays the same. It depends on the shape. Picture it turning in your head, and look at where its corners go. So turn each shape in your mind, and ask: would I notice that it had moved?

Longer or shorter? Compare them carefully: longer , shorter , taller , thinner . Tap the answer. Next question Compare them. Which is longer, taller or thinner? Tap the answer. To compare two lengths, start them at the same place. Line two pencils up at one end. The one that reaches further at the other end is longer, and the other one is shorter. For trees and people we say tall, taller and tallest. For a rope or a worm we can say thin, thinner and thinnest. Children look at only one end, or they choose the one that looks biggest overall. A thick worm is not a long worm. Check that the ends line up, then look at the other end. So line them up, look along to the far end, and then choose your word.

Heavier or lighter? Think about how heavy each thing is. Tap the answer. Next question Heavy, light, more and less. Think about how heavy each thing is, then tap the answer. On a balance, the heavier side always goes down. The lighter side goes up. If both sides weigh the same, the balance stays level. Big things are not always heavy. A big balloon is lighter than a small stone. Children think the bigger thing must be the heavier thing. Size can trick you. Look at which side goes down, or think about lifting it. So picture lifting each one in your hands, and feel which one pulls down more.

Pour and fill Think about how much each one holds : full , empty , more or less . Next question Full, empty, more and less. Think about how much water each one holds, then tap the answer. Capacity is how much something can hold. A bucket holds more than a cup, because it is bigger inside. When a container has no room left, it is full. When there is nothing in it, it is empty. Pour water from one jug into another, and the first one has less while the second has more. Children look only at how tall a container is. A tall thin glass can hold less than a wide bowl. Think about how much space there is inside. So picture pouring the water, and watch where it goes.

Read the numbers A ruler, scales, a jug and a thermometer all have a scale of numbers . Read them. Next question Every measuring tool has numbers on it. Read the numbers, then tap the answer. A measuring tool has a scale of numbers, and the numbers tell you how much. On a ruler, start at zero and see which number the end reaches. On a thermometer, the red line climbs higher, to bigger numbers, when it is hotter. On a measuring jug, more water reaches a bigger number. On scales, the pointer turns round to a bigger number for something heavier. Children start measuring from the end of the ruler instead of from zero. Line the thing up with zero first. Then read the number at the other end. So find zero, find where it stops, and read the number there.

Between, above, behind Tap the words that say where it is, or which way it is going: between, above, behind, towards. Next question Look at the picture. Tap the words that say where it is, or which way it is going. Position words say where something is, and direction words say which way it is going. Between means in the middle of two things. Above means higher up, and below means lower down. Behind means at the back, where it can be hidden. Towards means going closer, and away means going further off. Children mix up words that come in pairs, like above and below, or towards and away. Each word has a partner that means the opposite. Say both words, then decide which one fits. So point at the thing, look at what is next to it, and choose your word.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. No new ideas here. Every question uses something you have already done in this lesson. If it shows a shape, count the sides or ask whether you could hold it. If it asks about size, compare the two things. If it shows a clock, find the short hand first. Take your time. Read it, look at it, then tap.

Days of the week Tap the days in order, starting with Monday . Seven days make a week. Tap the days in order, starting with Monday. The days of the week always come round in the same order, and that order never changes. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Seven of them. Say them out loud with me, and after Sunday it starts at Monday again, round and round. Children start at whatever day it is today. The list on this screen always starts at Monday, whatever day it happens to be outside. So say the whole seven out loud from Monday, then tap them in that order.

Months of the year One month is missing. Which one belongs in the gap? Twelve months make a year. One month is missing. Tap the one that belongs in the gap. Twelve months make one year, and they always come in the same order too. January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December. One is missing from the line. Say the months out loud and listen for the one your voice says where the gap is. Children guess from what the missing month sounds like, or pick a month they like. Say the list instead. Your voice knows the order better than your guess does. So start at January and say them out loud until you reach the gap. Whatever you say there is the answer.

Short times and long times Tap them in order, from the shortest to the longest . A second is very short. A year is very long. Tap them in order, from the shortest to the longest. Some things take a tiny amount of time and some take a very long time. A second is about as long as saying one elephant. A minute is sixty of those. An hour is long enough for a film. A day is one whole sleep to the next. A week is seven days, and a year is all twelve months. Children put them in the order they meet them in the day, rather than by how long they last. Order them by length of time, from the shortest to the longest. So start with the very shortest one you can find, then keep asking which of the ones left is shortest now.

Telling the time The short hand tells the hour. When the long hand points to 12, it is something o'clock . Press Next hour . Next hour A clock. The short hand tells the hour. When the long hand points to twelve, it is something o'clock. Press next hour. A clock has two hands, and they do two different jobs. The short hand tells you the hour. The long hand tells you how far through the hour you are. When the long hand points straight up to twelve, the hour has just begun, and we say o clock. If the short hand is on three and the long hand is on twelve, it is three o clock. When the long hand points straight down to six, we are halfway through, and we say half past. Children read the long hand as the hour, because it is bigger and easier to see. It is the short hand that tells you the hour, every time. So find the short hand first and see which number it is nearest. Then look at the long hand to see whether it is o clock or half past.

How long does it take? Think about how long each thing takes: a second , a minute , an hour , a day , a week or a year . Next question Seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years. Think about how long each thing takes, then tap the answer. We use different words for short times and long times. A blink takes less than a second. Eating a banana takes a few minutes. A night of sleep lasts many hours. A school holiday lasts weeks, and there are twelve months in a year. Children think something that feels long must take a long time, like waiting for a treat. Waiting can feel long even when it is only a few minutes. Think about the clock, not the feeling. So picture doing the thing, and ask: is that seconds, minutes, hours, days, or longer?

Find the clock Read each clock. The long hand says o'clock or half past , and the short hand tells the hour. Next question Read each clock. The short hand tells the hour, and the long hand says o'clock or half past. Tap the answer. Every clock tells the time the same way, with its two hands. The long hand pointing straight up to twelve means o clock. The long hand pointing straight down to six means half past. The short hand tells you which hour. At half past, the short hand sits halfway between two numbers. Children read the long hand as the hour, because it is the bigger hand. The long hand only says o clock or half past. It is the short hand that tells you the hour. So look at the long hand first, to see o clock or half past, and then read the short hand.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. No new ideas here. Every question uses something you have already done in this lesson. If it shows a shape, count the sides or ask whether you could hold it. If it asks about size, compare the two things. If it shows a clock, find the short hand first. Take your time. Read it, look at it, then tap.

Ask everyone Our question is: which fruit do you like best? Tap each child to hear their answer. Ask everyone the question. Tap each child to hear the answer, and watch the answers line up in rows. Before you can draw anything, you need answers. Asking everyone the same question is how you get them. Our question is which fruit do you like best. Tap Amina and she tells you her answer. Tap Musa and he tells you his. Keep going until every child has been asked. Then you have twelve answers, one from each child. Children often tap the same child twice, or stop partway because it feels done. Then the numbers are wrong, and every chart you build after this is wrong too. So tap each child once. When you think you have finished, check that nobody is left.

Write a list A list writes down every answer, one under the other. Here are the answers written as a list. Read down the list and count. A list writes every answer down, one under the other, in the order you got them. Amina said pineapple, so pineapple goes first. Musa said banana, so banana goes underneath. Twelve children, twelve lines. To find how many liked pineapple, you read down the list and count every pineapple you see. A list is long, and it is easy to lose your place. Children count the same line twice, or skip one without noticing. So put your finger on each line as you count it and slide it down. Your finger keeps your place.

Make a table A table says each answer once, with how many chose it. A table is shorter than a list. It says each answer once, with how many children chose it. One number is missing. A table is shorter than a list. Each answer is written once, with a number beside it saying how many children chose it. The list had pineapple written on five separate lines. The table writes pineapple once, and puts five next to it. Same answers, far less writing. One number is missing here, so count that fruit in the list and fill it in. Here is the slip. Children read the number as how many kinds of fruit there are. It is not. The number beside pineapple is how many children, not how many pineapples. So find the row with the gap, count that answer in the list, and put in the number you counted.

Build a block graph One block stands for one child . Press + to add a block. Build the block graph. Press the plus under a fruit to add one block for one child. A block graph turns the numbers into towers. One block means one child. Five children chose pineapple, so the pineapple tower needs five blocks. Press the plus under pineapple five times and watch it grow. Do that for every fruit, and the towers match the table exactly. Children press the plus until the tower looks about right, instead of counting. A tower that looks tall is not the same as a tower with the right number of blocks in it. So say the number out loud first. Then press the plus that many times, counting as you go.

Read the block graph Look at the graph, then tap the answer. Now read the graph. Which is the tallest? Which is the shortest? Tap the answer. Once the graph is built, you can answer questions just by looking at it. The tallest tower is the one most children chose. The shortest is the one fewest chose. You do not have to count every block to see that. Just look at which tower reaches highest. Watch this one. Tallest means most children chose it. It does not mean the biggest fruit, and it does not mean the best fruit. The graph only knows what people said. So run your eye along the tops of the towers. Find the highest. Tap its name.

Make a pictogram A pictogram uses a picture instead of a block. A pictogram uses a little picture instead of a block. One picture stands for one child. A pictogram is the same idea as a block graph, with a little picture instead of a block. Here one picture stands for one child. Five children chose pineapple, so there are five pineapple pictures in that row. Count the pictures and you have your number. Children count the rows instead of the pictures, or think a bigger picture must mean more. Every picture here is worth the same. One picture, one child. So point at each picture in the row and count them one by one.

Sort into a hoop Tap the cards that follow the rule. A hoop holds the things that follow the rule. Tap a card to put it in the hoop. A hoop is a ring that holds the things which follow one rule. Everything else stays outside it. If the rule is red, then every red card goes inside the hoop, and every card that is not red stays out. Look at your card, ask does it follow the rule, then decide. Children put a card in because they like it, or because it looks a bit similar to the others. The hoop does not care about any of that. Only the rule decides. So read the rule again, look at your card, and ask yourself one question. Does it follow.

A Venn diagram Where does this card go? not red and not a circle This is a Venn diagram: two hoops that cross over. A card that follows both rules goes in the middle, where the hoops overlap. Two hoops, crossing over, with a space in the middle. Two hoops that cross like this are called a Venn diagram. Each hoop has its own rule. Say one hoop is red and the other is round. A red square follows the red rule only, so it goes in the red hoop. A blue circle follows the round rule only. A red circle follows both rules at once, so it goes in the middle where the hoops cross. A blue square follows neither, so it stays outside both. The middle is where children slip. They think it means a bit of one and a bit of the other. It does not. It means both rules, at the same time, in the same card. So ask two questions. Is it red. Is it round. Two yeses means the middle.

A Carroll diagram Which box does this card belong in? A Carroll diagram has boxes instead of hoops. Every card has a box of its own. Where does this one go? A Carroll diagram does the same job as the hoops, using boxes instead. There are four boxes. Red and round. Red and not round. Not red and round. Not red and not round. Every card belongs in exactly one of them. A red circle goes in red and round. Children hunt for a box that is nearly right. There is always exactly one box that fits, so if two of them seem to fit, you have read one of the labels wrongly. So answer the two questions, yes or no, then find the box with those two answers on it.

Answer the question Read the graph and tap the answer. Here is a graph about pets. Every question has one right answer, and the graph tells you what it is. A graph is built to answer questions. The answer is in the picture, not in your head. Here is a graph about pets. If it asks how many children have a cat, find the cat tower and count it. If it asks which pet is most popular, find the tallest tower. Children answer with what they think, or with their own favourite pet. Your favourite is not in this graph. Only what these children said is. So read the question, find the part of the graph it is asking about, and read the answer straight off the graph.

What can we say? Only one of these is true . Tap it. What can we really say about this graph? Only one of these is true. Tap it. A graph tells you some things and stays completely silent about others. Only some sentences are true. Say the graph shows six children have a dog and two have a fish. More children have a dog than a fish is true, and you can point at it. Dogs are better than fish is not true, because the graph never said that. And how many children have no pet at all is not there either, because nobody was asked. This is the hardest step in the lesson. A sentence can sound completely sensible and still not be something the graph shows. Sounding right is not the same as being on the graph. So take each sentence and ask one thing. Can I point at the part of the graph that proves it.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. No new ideas here. Every question uses something you have already done in this lesson. If the question shows you a graph, read the answer off the graph. If it asks about a hoop or a box, check the rule and answer yes or no. Take your time. Read it, look at it, then tap.
